title: US government says hackers are now exploiting critical PHP web bugs | TechCrunch
body: U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA has confirmed that hackers are now actively exploiting a pair of critical security vulnerabilities in the widely used PHP web software and has ordered civilian federal agencies within the U.S. government to fix their systems within the next three days. [...] While the bugs are rated critical, meaning they can be highly damaging if exploited, security researchers said that developing a working exploit to hack into vulnerable systems was initially challenging — but not impossible. Confirmed in-the-wild exploitation now puts extra pressure on organizations to patch their systems to prevent malicious compromises, disruption, and data breaches. [...] The two bugs in PHP are among countless vulnerabilities that have not yet been discovered or have been deprioritized for years but now pose a risk due to advances in AI models’ ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities, including by chaining multiple flaws together.

title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware threatens most servers on planet Earth - Ars Technica
body: The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install [...] There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear. [...] CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail, stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot

title: TSMC Says AI Chip Demand Is Still Far Above What It Can Supply. That's Why I'd Buy Nvidia Stock. | The Motley Fool

Nvidia (NVDA -1.43%) investors got a new look at the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) chips on Thursday, Oct. 15. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -2.28%), which makes chip wafers for Nvidia, posted third-quarter revenue of $46.7 billion -- over the high end of the $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion range management had forecast in July.

And TSMC's chairman and CEO, C.C. Wei, didn't sound worried about what's next. [...] Showing how much AI is powering the chipmaker, TSMC's revenue from high-performance computing (the platform that includes AI chips) climbed 22% sequentially in the third quarter. That was faster than the platform's 20% sequential growth in the second quarter. High-performance computing is now 68% of TSMC's revenue, up from 57% in the third quarter of 2025. Overall, TSMC's revenue grew 41% year over year in U.S. dollars. Net income, which TSMC reports in New Taiwan dollars, rose 69%.

title: Chips and Chokepoints: Chris Miller on the Geopolitics of the AI Supply Chain - Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology - Carnegie Mellon University
body: In his February 26 lecture, entitled “Geopolitics of AI Supply Chains,” Miller focused on the importance of the technology, why supply chain bottlenecks exist, how they emerged, and the underlying relationship dynamics at play. He argued that no issue is more pressing today than the relationship between the world’s two largest economies—the United States and China—and their militaries in the context of the AI supply chain. [...] Beyond technical bottlenecks, Miller contended that the semiconductor landscape is being reshaped by the demands of global political leaders seeking to align supply chains with their own national interests. Miller previously traced this power struggle in his 2022 New York Times bestseller, Chip War, which underscores how control over computing power has historically dictated military and economic advantage. This trend has only intensified in 2026, as evidenced by the rising use of tariffs and [...] What makes this technology unique, Miller argued, is a reliance on supply chains that—for the first time in history—cannot be managed by a single nation. Instead, these goods are produced across multiple countries and continents. “Today there's not a single country in the world that can produce, not even an advanced chip, but a moderately advanced chip on its own,” he said.
